History & Physical (Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
65-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presents via tele-consult with a 5-day history of dry cough every 20–30 min and continuous greenish rhinorrhoea, accompanied by subjective fever/chills and myalgias; no dyspnoea or chest pain. Clinical impression is viral upper-respiratory infection; provided symptomatic advice and safety-netting.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Dry, non-productive cough and “streaming” nose.  
• Onset & course: Began ~5 days ago; symptoms persist, not clearly improving.  
• Character: Cough is dry, occurs every 20–30 min. Nasal discharge described as “pretty green.”  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Subjective fever (feels hot to touch) alternating with chills; temperature not measured.  
  – Generalised muscle aches.  
  – Brief episode of diarrhoea at onset; resolved.  
• Negative/pertinent review of systems:  
  – No sputum production, haemoptysis, chest pain, dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, wheeze.  
  – No sore throat, ear pain, rash, headache, visual changes.  
  – Eating/drinking and urine output normal; no current vomiting or diarrhoea.  
• Self-care: Takes 2–3 sachets/day of Lemsip (paracetamol-containing cold remedy); provides temporary throat relief. No other OTC medications.  
• Exacerbating/relieving factors: Lemsip soothes throat; no other factors described.

Past Medical History:
• Type 2 diabetes mellitus – most recent routine bloods 3 weeks ago reported “normal.”  
• Hypertension – blood-pressure follow-up overdue; last BP result unknown.  
• No chronic respiratory disease.  

Medications:
• Metformin – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Lisinopril – patient believes “200” (likely mis-stated); exact dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Lemsip (paracetamol combination) PRN 2–3 sachets daily.

Allergies:
• No known drug allergies.  
• Seasonal hay-fever (non-drug).

Social History:
• Lives with partner and a dog.  
• Occupation: Office manager.  
• Smoking: Not documented.  
• Alcohol: “Odd sherry” only (occasional).  
• Recreational drugs: Not mentioned.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Not performed – remote video consultation.  
• No vital signs provided.

Investigations:
• None performed during consult.  
• Patient reports “normal” diabetes blood tests 3 weeks prior (details not available).

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Acute viral upper respiratory tract infection / viral bronchitis (most likely):  
• Assessment: 5-day history of dry cough, rhinorrhoea, myalgias, subjective fever; no red-flag lower-respiratory features. Diabetes increases risk of secondary bacterial infection.  
• Plan:  
  – Encourage symptomatic care: adequate fluids, rest, continue Lemsip but avoid other paracetamol-containing products.  
  – Obtain digital thermometer; monitor temperature twice daily.  
  – Safety-net: seek reassessment if temp ≥ 37.5–38 °C persists or spikes, cough worsens, sputum becomes purulent or bloody, haemoptysis, dyspnoea, chest pain, or new nasal bleeding.  
  – If deterioration or prolonged fever, consider in-person review and possible antibiotics.  

Issue 2 – Chronic disease management (diabetes, hypertension):  
• Assessment: Routine monitoring appears delayed; patient lacks home glucose monitoring kit.  
• Plan:  
  – Arrange/attend scheduled GP appointments for BP and diabetes checks.  
  – Consider provision of glucometer if not already supplied (primary-care follow-up).

Issue 3 – Patient education / medication safety:  
• Plan:  
  – Advise against daytime cough suppressants; limited use at night if sleep disturbed.  
  – Highlight paracetamol content in Lemsip to prevent accidental overdose.  
  – Encourage smoking abstinence if applicable and adherence to healthy lifestyle.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute viral URTI / influenza-like illness – High likelihood: Classical constellation of abrupt dry cough, rhinorrhoea, myalgias, subjective fever; no focal chest signs.  
2. COVID-19 infection – Moderate likelihood: Symptom overlap and current prevalence; lacks anosmia/dyspnoea but testing may still be warranted if clinically indicated.  
3. Acute bacterial sinusitis – Moderate to low likelihood: Green nasal discharge > 5 days suggests possible bacterial superinfection, but absent sinus pain/tenderness and systemic toxicity.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: objective vitals, smoking status clarification, detailed medication doses, allergy confirmation to food/latex, vaccination status.  
● Transcript vs DDx conflicts: None significant; DDx supportive.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; occasional minor inaudible words but clinical content preserved.
